questions.title: Profiling Java Applications
questions.question: How do you profile a Java application to find performance bottlenecks?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Async profiling (async-profiler): low-overhead CPU profiling — safe in production**
- **Flame graphs: visualize where CPU time is spent — wide blocks = hot methods**
- **Thread dumps: `jstack` or `jcmd Thread.print` — diagnose deadlocks, thread starvation**
- **VisualVM / JProfiler: full GUI profiling — better in staging than production**
- **JFR (Java Flight Recorder): low-overhead continuous recording built into JDK**
- **Micrometer timers: instrument your own hot paths with code-level metrics**

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Performance profiling is about measuring before optimizing. The first step is identifying whether the bottleneck is CPU (high CPU, slow computation), I/O (threads waiting on DB or network), or garbage collection (frequent GC pauses). Monitoring metrics give you this picture — Micrometer exposes CPU, GC, thread, and memory metrics.

For CPU profiling, async-profiler is the tool of choice — it's low-overhead and safe to run in production. It produces flame graphs where the width of each block represents the proportion of CPU time that method took. Wide blocks at the top of the flame are your bottlenecks.

For I/O and thread issues, thread dumps are invaluable — `jcmd <pid> Thread.print` gives a snapshot of every thread's current stack trace. If you see 50 threads all blocked on `SocketInputStream.read()`, you have I/O bottleneck, not CPU. If you see circular waits, you have a deadlock.

Java Flight Recorder (JFR) is the continuous recording option — minimal overhead, always on, captures events over time.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Profiling Workflow

```bash
# STEP 1: Identify the problem type from metrics
# CPU > 80%: CPU-bound → use CPU profiler (async-profiler)
# CPU < 20%, threads BLOCKED/WAITING: I/O-bound → thread dump + DB analysis
# Frequent Full GC, growing heap: Memory → heap dump analysis
# High response time variability: GC pauses → GC log analysis

# STEP 2a: CPU Profiling with async-profiler
# Download: https://github.com/async-profiler/async-profiler

# Profile for 60 seconds, output flame graph:
./asprof -d 60 -f /tmp/flamegraph.html <pid>

# Or attach to running JVM:
./asprof start <pid>
sleep 60
./asprof stop -f /tmp/flamegraph.html <pid>

# Profile allocation (find what's allocating most):
./asprof -e alloc -d 60 -f /tmp/alloc.html <pid>

# STEP 2b: Thread dump for I/O / deadlock analysis:
jcmd <pid> Thread.print > /tmp/threads.txt
# OR:
jstack <pid> > /tmp/threads.txt

# STEP 2c: Java Flight Recorder (JFR):
# Enable on startup:
java -XX:StartFlightRecording=filename=/tmp/recording.jfr,\
     duration=60s,settings=profile -jar myapp.jar

# Trigger recording on running app:
jcmd <pid> JFR.start duration=60s filename=/tmp/recording.jfr
# Open in JDK Mission Control (JMC) for analysis
```

## Reading Flame Graphs

```
FLAME GRAPH READING GUIDE:

  Width of block = % of CPU time spent in that method (and its callees)
  Height = call depth (bottom = main, top = leaf methods)

  HOT SPOT EXAMPLE:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                   CPU TIME (100%)                    │
  ├───────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┤
  │  Jackson.serialize()  │  Other stuff (45%)           │
  │  (55% of CPU time!)   │                              │
  ├────────────────────┬──┤                              │
  │ObjectMapper.write()│  │                              │
  ├────────────────────┤  │                              │
  │JsonGenerator      │  │                              │
  └───────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────┘

  → Jackson serialization taking 55% of CPU
  → FIX: Use Jackson streaming API, pre-configure ObjectMapper,
          or reduce serialization frequency

  ANOTHER PATTERN — I/O waits (not CPU):
  If flame graph shows mostly WAITING state in threads
  → threads blocked waiting for I/O, not consuming CPU
  → CPU profiler won't help — use thread dump + DB EXPLAIN ANALYZE
```

## Thread Dump Analysis

```
THREAD DUMP SECTIONS:

Normal state (RUNNABLE executing code):
"http-nio-8080-exec-1" #25 daemon prio=5
   java.lang.Thread.State: RUNNABLE
   at com.example.OrderService.calculateTotal(OrderService.java:45)
   at com.example.OrderController.createOrder(OrderController.java:78)

Blocked on DB (normal for DB calls):
"http-nio-8080-exec-2" #26 daemon prio=5
   java.lang.Thread.State: RUNNABLE
   at java.net.SocketInputStream.read(Native Method)  ← Waiting for DB response
   at org.postgresql.core.QueryExecutor.execute(...)

Blocked on lock (potential deadlock):
"http-nio-8080-exec-3"
   java.lang.Thread.State: BLOCKED (on object monitor)
   waiting to lock <0x7f45b1c23400> (a com.example.OrderService)
   at com.example.OrderService.reserve(...)
   - owned by: "http-nio-8080-exec-7"  ← exec-7 owns the lock exec-3 needs

"http-nio-8080-exec-7"
   java.lang.Thread.State: BLOCKED
   waiting to lock <0x7f45b1c23401> (a com.example.InventoryService)
   at com.example.InventoryService.update(...)
   - owned by: "http-nio-8080-exec-3"  ← DEADLOCK! 3 waits on 7, 7 waits on 3

DEADLOCK FOUND:
  exec-3 owns lock A, waiting for lock B
  exec-7 owns lock B, waiting for lock A → DEADLOCK
  FIX: Always acquire locks in the same order, or use tryLock() with timeout
```

## Instrumentation with Micrometer

```java
// Add timing to your hot paths:
@Service
public class OrderService {

    private final MeterRegistry meterRegistry;
    private final Timer orderCreationTimer;
    private final Counter orderErrorCounter;

    public OrderService(MeterRegistry meterRegistry) {
        this.meterRegistry = meterRegistry;
        this.orderCreationTimer = Timer.builder("order.creation")
            .description("Time to create an order")
            .tag("service", "order")
            .publishPercentiles(0.5, 0.95, 0.99)  // Percentiles
            .register(meterRegistry);
        this.orderErrorCounter = Counter.builder("order.errors")
            .tag("type", "creation")
            .register(meterRegistry);
    }

    public Order createOrder(CreateOrderRequest request) {
        return orderCreationTimer.recordCallable(() -> {
            // All the work happens here — timed automatically
            Order order = buildOrder(request);
            validateInventory(order);
            processPayment(order);
            return orderRepository.save(order);
        });
    }
}
// Prometheus metrics exposed at /actuator/prometheus:
// order_creation_seconds_count, order_creation_seconds_sum
// order_creation_seconds{quantile="0.95"} 0.245  ← p95 latency: 245ms
```

## Production Reality

async-profiler is the go-to tool for production CPU profiling — it uses perf_events or AsyncGetCallTrace to sample with < 2% overhead and doesn't suffer the safepoint bias of earlier JVM profilers (which only sample at safepoints, missing some hot paths). For continuous observability, enable JFR with a low-overhead settings profile (`settings=jdk.jfr.consumer.defaults`) — it captures GC events, thread events, exceptions, and lock waits continuously with < 1% overhead. Enable it by default in production.
